questions.question: Explain macronutrient deficiencies in AIDS.
questions.solution_html: • Explain macronutrient deficiencies in AIDS. / ● Definition/Overview: In Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome, macronutrient deficiencies occur due to increased metabolic demands, poor intake, and malabsorption – (1 mark) ● Causes: Reduced appetite, infections, malabsorption, drug side effects, and increased energy/protein needs – (1 mark) ● Protein deficiency: Leads to muscle wasting, weight loss, weakened immunity (cachexia) – (1 mark) ● Energy (carbohydrate & fat) deficiency: Causes fatigue, severe weight loss, and loss of body fat stores – (1 mark) ● Consequences/Management: Leads to wasting syndrome; managed by high-calorie, high-protein diet, nutritional support, and treatment of infections – (1 mark)

questions.question: Explain the dietary guidelines for managing gastritis.
questions.solution_html: • Explain the dietary guidelines for managing gastritis. / Dietary guidelines for managing gastritis ● Eat small, frequent meals – avoids excess gastric acid secretion and reduces stomach irritation (1 mark) ● Avoid irritant foods – such as spicy, fried, oily, and highly seasoned foods, which increase gastric inflammation (1 mark) ● Limit gastric acid stimulants – avoid caffeine, alcohol, and carbonated beverages (1 mark) ● Include bland, easily digestible foods – such as boiled rice, soft cereals, curd, and well-cooked vegetables (1 mark) ● Maintain healthy eating habits & lifestyle – regular meal timing, avoid skipping meals, reduce stress, and avoid smoking (1 mark)

questions.question: Describe the complications of AIDS. Part D Essay
questions.solution_html: • Describe the complications of AIDS. / Complications of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome ● Opportunistic infections – due to weakened immunity (e.g., tuberculosis, pneumonia, fungal infections) – (1 mark) ● Cancers – increased risk of malignancies such as Kaposi’s sarcoma and lymphoma – (1 mark) ● Severe weight loss (wasting syndrome) – progressive loss of body weight and muscle mass – (1 mark) ● Neurological complications – memory loss, confusion, neuropathy, and dementia – (1 mark) ● Organ failure / multi-system involvement – chronic damage to lungs, liver, and other organs leading to death if untreated – (1 mark) Part D Essay Answer any 2 questions Each question carries (10 marks)

questions.question: Explain biochemical and immune tests used in food allergy diagnosis.
questions.solution_html: • Explain biochemical and immune tests used in food allergy diagnosis. / Biochemical and immune tests used in food allergy diagnosis A. Biochemical tests (5 marks) ● Serum histamine level test – Measures histamine released during allergic reaction (1 mark) ● Tryptase level test – Elevated in mast cell activation/anaphylaxis (1 mark) ● Eosinophil count (CBC) – Increased eosinophils indicate allergic response (1 mark) ● IgE-related biochemical estimation (total IgE) – Indicates allergic tendency (1 mark) ● Mediator release tests (e.g., leukotrienes) – Detect inflammatory mediators in allergy (1 mark) B. Immune (immunological) tests (5 marks) ● Skin prick test (SPT) – Allergen applied to skin; wheal indicates IgE-mediated allergy (1 mark) ● Specific IgE test (RAST / ImmunoCAP) – Measures allergen-specific IgE antibodies in blood (1 mark) ● Elimination diet and oral food challenge – Gold standard for identifying trigger foods (1 mark) ● Basophil activation test (BAT) – Measures activation of basophils on exposure to allergens (1 mark) ● Patch test (for delayed allergy reactions) – Detects non-IgE mediated hypersensitivity (1 mark)

questions.question: Explain malaria with causes, symptoms and types of fever.
questions.solution_html: • Explain malaria with causes, symptoms and types of fever. / Malaria – causes, symptoms and types of fever A. Definition (1 mark) ● Malaria is a mosquito-borne infectious disease caused by Plasmodium parasites and transmitted by female Anopheles mosquito. B. Causes / Etiology (3 marks) ● Infection by Plasmodium species (e.g., P. vivax, P. falciparum, P. malariae, P. ovale ) – (1 mark) ● Transmission through bite of infected female Anopheles mosquito – (1 mark) ● Parasite multiplies in liver and red blood cells causing fever episodes – (1 mark) C. Symptoms (3 marks) ● High fever with chills and rigor – (1 mark) ● Headache, body ache, fatigue, and sweating – (1 mark) ● Nausea, vomiting, anemia, and splenomegaly – (1 mark) D. Types of fever pattern in malaria (3 marks) ● Tertian fever – fever every 48 hours (seen in P. vivax, P. ovale ) – (1 mark) ● Quartan fever – fever every 72 hours (seen in P. malariae ) – (1 mark) ● Irregular or malignant fever – seen in P. falciparum , often severe and continuous – (1 mark) .

questions.question: Discuss the dietary management of diarrhoea.
questions.solution_html: • Discuss the dietary management of diarrhoea. / A. Definition / Aim of diet (1 mark) ● Dietary management of diarrhoea aims to replace fluids and electrolytes, reduce intestinal irritation, and restore normal bowel function – (1 mark) B. Fluid and electrolyte replacement (2 marks) ● Increase intake of oral rehydration solutions (ORS), coconut water, clear soups – (1 mark) ● Maintain hydration to prevent dehydration and electrolyte imbalance (sodium, potassium loss) – (1 mark) C. Energy and protein intake (2 marks) ● Provide easily digestible, high-energy foods like rice, banana, potatoes – (1 mark) ● Include moderate protein sources like curd, dal water, eggs (if tolerated) – (1 mark) D. Foods to include (2 marks) ● Low-fiber, bland diet (BRAT diet: banana, rice, apple, toast) – (1 mark) ● Cooked cereals, boiled vegetables, yogurt/probiotics to restore gut flora – (1 mark) E. Foods to avoid (2 marks) ● Avoid spicy, fatty, fried foods and caffeine (irritate gut) – (1 mark) ● Avoid milk (in lactose intolerance), raw vegetables, carbonated drinks – (1 mark) F. Feeding guidelines / general advice (1 mark) ● Give small frequent meals, maintain hygiene, and gradually return to normal diet after recovery – (1 mark)

questions.final_answer: Discuss the dietary management of diarrhoea. A. Definition / Aim of diet ● Dietary management of diarrhoea aims to replace fluids and electrolytes, reduce intestinal irritation, and restore normal bowel function – B. Fluid and electrolyte replacement ● Increase intake of oral rehydration solutions (ORS), coconut water, clear soups – ● Maintain hydration to prevent dehydration and electrolyte imbalance (sodium, potassium loss) – C. Energy and protein intake ● Provide easily digestible, high-energy foods like rice, banana, potatoes – ● Include moderate protein sources like curd, dal water, eggs (if tolerated) – D. Foods to include ● Low-fiber, bland diet (BRAT diet: banana, rice, apple, toast) – ● Cooked cereals, boiled vegetables, yogurt/probiotics to restore gut flora – E. Foods to avoid ● Avoid spicy, fatty, fried foods and caffeine (irritate gut) – ● Avoid milk (in lactose intolerance), raw vegetables, carbonated drinks – F. Feeding guidelines / general advice ● Give small frequent meals, maintain hygiene, and gradually return to normal diet after recovery
